title: What Is System Design?
intro: System design is planning how the parts of a software system fit together so it stays fast, reliable and affordable as it grows. This series builds it up one concept at a time.

slides.heading: The big picture
slides.subtitle: Designing the whole system, not one function.
slides.explain: Coding answers "how do I build this feature?". System design answers "how do servers, databases, caches and queues work together for millions of users?"
points: Decide which components you need
Decide how they talk to each other
Plan for growth and failure

slides.heading: Functional needs
slides.subtitle: What the system must do.
slides.explain: These are the features users see. List them first, because every design decision should serve one of them.
points: Users can sign up and log in
Users can post a photo
Users can scroll a feed

slides.heading: Non-functional needs
slides.subtitle: How well the system must do it.
slides.explain: These qualities shape the architecture. Two apps with the same features can need very different designs because of them.
points: Scalability: handle more users
Availability: stay up, e.g. 99.9% uptime
Latency: respond quickly
Durability: never lose data

slides.heading: Estimate the scale
slides.subtitle: Back-of-the-envelope math.
slides.explain: Rough numbers tell you whether one server is enough or you need hundreds. You only need the right order of magnitude, not exact figures.
points: 10M daily users x 10 requests = 100M requests a day
That's about 1,150 requests per second on average
Peaks can be several times higher

slides.heading: Trade-offs
slides.subtitle: There is no perfect design.
slides.explain: Faster reads can mean slower writes, and more consistency can mean less availability. Good design means choosing the right trade-off and explaining why.
points: Speed vs cost
Consistency vs availability
Simplicity vs flexibility

scenario.situation: A team builds a photo app without writing down requirements or estimating traffic.
scenario.problem: It runs on one server and one database. A viral post brings 50x the usual traffic and the whole app goes down.
scenario.fix: Start with requirements and rough numbers. Knowing the expected peak would have shown the need for caching and more servers before launch.
scenario.takeaway: Requirements and estimates come before architecture.

cta: What system would you like us to design later in this series?

title: How a Web Request Travels
intro: Before scaling anything, you need to know the path a single request takes. Every later part of this series adds a component to this path.

slides.heading: The client
slides.subtitle: Where every request starts.
slides.explain: The client is the browser or mobile app. It doesn't know where your servers are; it only knows a domain name like api.example.com.
points: Sends HTTP requests
Shows the response to the user

slides.heading: DNS
slides.subtitle: Finding the server's address.
slides.explain: DNS turns the domain name into an IP address, like a phone book. The answer is cached, so this step is usually skipped on repeat visits.
points: api.example.com becomes an IP address
Cached by the browser, OS and resolvers

slides.heading: The app server
slides.subtitle: Where your code runs.
slides.explain: The server receives the request, runs your business logic, such as checking a password or building a feed, and decides what data it needs.
points: Runs your backend code
Validates input and checks permissions
Talks to the database
examples: Node.js, Django or Spring Boot apps

slides.heading: The database
slides.subtitle: Where data lives permanently.
slides.explain: The server reads or writes data in the database, then sends the result back to the client, usually as JSON.
points: Stores users, posts and orders
Often the slowest step in a request

slides.heading: The full path
slides.subtitle: One request, end to end.
slides.explain: The client looks up DNS, connects to the server, the server queries the database, and the response travels back. Each hop adds time, which is why later parts add caches and CDNs.
points: Every hop adds latency
Every component can fail

scenario.situation: A page takes 3 seconds to load and the team wants to make it faster.
scenario.problem: Without knowing the request path, they spend a week optimizing frontend code that only took 100 milliseconds.
scenario.fix: Timing each hop shows one database query takes 2.5 seconds. Adding an index removes most of the delay.
scenario.takeaway: Know the request path before you optimize.

cta: Which part of the request path do you think is usually slowest?

title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
intro: When one server can't keep up, you have two choices: make it bigger, or add more of them.

slides.heading: The problem
slides.subtitle: One server has limits.
slides.explain: Every server has a fixed amount of CPU, memory and network. As traffic grows, response times climb until requests start timing out.
points: CPU hits 100%
Memory runs out
Requests queue up and slow down

slides.heading: Vertical scaling
slides.subtitle: Make the server bigger.
slides.explain: Also called scaling up: move to a machine with more CPU and RAM. It needs no code changes, so it's the quickest first fix.
points: Simple: no architecture changes
Has a ceiling: machines only get so big
Still a single point of failure

slides.heading: Horizontal scaling
slides.subtitle: Add more servers.
slides.explain: Also called scaling out: run many copies of your app and share traffic between them. This is how large systems keep growing.
points: Grows far beyond one machine
If one server dies, others keep serving
Needs a load balancer in front

slides.heading: Stateless servers
slides.subtitle: The key to scaling out.
slides.explain: If a server keeps user sessions in its own memory, the next request may hit a different server that knows nothing. Keep servers stateless and store shared state elsewhere.
points: Store sessions in Redis or a database
Any server can handle any request

slides.heading: Which to choose?
slides.subtitle: Usually both, in order.
slides.explain: Most teams scale up first because it's easy, then scale out when they hit limits or need high availability.
points: Early stage: scale up
Growing fast: scale out
Need high uptime: scale out

scenario.situation: An e-commerce site runs on one large server before a big sale.
scenario.problem: They upgrade to the biggest machine available. Sale traffic still exceeds it, and when it crashes the whole store is offline.
scenario.fix: Run several smaller stateless servers behind a load balancer and add more during the sale. One crash no longer takes the site down.
scenario.takeaway: Scale up for simplicity; scale out for growth and uptime.

cta: Has your app ever outgrown its server?

title: Load Balancers Explained
intro: Once you have more than one server, something has to decide which server handles each request. That's the load balancer.

slides.heading: What it does
slides.subtitle: A traffic manager for your servers.
slides.explain: The load balancer sits between users and your servers. Users connect to one address, and it forwards each request to a healthy server behind it.
points: One public address for many servers
Spreads load across them

slides.heading: Algorithms
slides.subtitle: How it picks a server.
slides.explain: Different strategies suit different workloads. Round robin is the simplest; least connections copes better when some requests take much longer.
points: Round robin: servers take turns
Least connections: pick the least busy
IP hash: same client, same server

slides.heading: Health checks
slides.subtitle: Avoiding broken servers.
slides.explain: The load balancer regularly checks each server. If one stops responding, it's taken out of rotation until it recovers, so users don't hit it.
points: Detects failed servers automatically
Makes zero-downtime deploys possible

slides.heading: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
slides.subtitle: How deep it looks.
slides.explain: A Layer 4 balancer routes by IP and port only, so it's very fast. A Layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by URL path or headers.
points: L4: fast and simple
L7: smart routing, e.g. /api to API servers

slides.heading: Don't add a weak spot
slides.subtitle: The balancer can fail too.
slides.explain: If the load balancer goes down, everything behind it does too. Production setups run at least two, or use a managed cloud load balancer.
points: Run redundant load balancers
Managed options handle this for you

scenario.situation: A site runs three servers behind a round-robin load balancer, and one server's disk fills up.
scenario.problem: Without health checks, one in three requests still goes to the broken server, so a third of users see errors.
scenario.fix: Turn on health checks. The balancer notices the failing server within seconds and sends traffic only to the two healthy ones.
scenario.takeaway: A load balancer without health checks spreads failures too.

cta: Do you use Nginx, a cloud load balancer, or something else?

title: Caching in System Design
intro: The fastest request is one that never reaches your database. Caching keeps frequently used data somewhere much faster.

slides.heading: Why cache?
slides.subtitle: Memory beats database queries.
slides.explain: Reading from an in-memory cache like Redis typically takes under a millisecond, while database queries often take far longer. Caching hot data cuts latency and database load.
points: Faster responses
Less load on the database
Lower cost at scale

slides.heading: Cache-aside
slides.subtitle: The most common pattern.
slides.explain: The app checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads from the database, saves the result in the cache, then returns it. The next request is a hit.
points: Simple and widely used
Only caches data that's requested
The first request after a miss is slow

slides.heading: Write-through
slides.subtitle: Write to both at once.
slides.explain: Every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always current. The trade-off is slower writes.
points: Cache stays up to date
Writes take a little longer
Good for data read right after writing

slides.heading: Expiry & eviction
slides.subtitle: Caches can't keep everything.
slides.explain: A TTL removes entries after a set time so stale data doesn't live forever. When memory fills up, a policy like LRU removes the least recently used items.
points: TTL: expire after N seconds
LRU: drop the least recently used
Hit rate shows how well it works

slides.heading: Invalidation
slides.subtitle: The hard part.
slides.explain: When the real data changes, the cached copy is wrong until it's updated or removed. Many systems delete the cache key on every write and keep a TTL as a safety net.
points: Delete the key when data changes
Keep a TTL as a backup
Stale data is the main risk

scenario.situation: A news site's homepage runs the same heavy database query for every visitor.
scenario.problem: During breaking news, thousands of identical queries per second overload the database and pages time out.
scenario.fix: Cache the homepage data in Redis with a 30-second TTL. The database now runs that query about twice a minute instead of thousands of times a second.
scenario.takeaway: Cache data that's read often and changes rarely.

cta: Redis, Memcached, or something else in your stack?

title: Database Replication
intro: One database is a single point of failure and a read bottleneck. Replication keeps copies of your data on several machines.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.subtitle: Copies of the same data.
slides.explain: Replication continuously copies data from one database server to others. If one machine fails, another still has the data, and reads can be spread across the copies.
points: Protects against hardware failure
Spreads read traffic

slides.heading: Primary-replica
slides.subtitle: One writer, many readers.
slides.explain: All writes go to the primary. Replicas copy its changes and serve reads. Most apps read far more than they write, so this scales well.
points: Writes: primary only
Reads: any replica
Add replicas to scale reads

slides.heading: Replication lag
slides.subtitle: Replicas can be slightly behind.
slides.explain: With asynchronous replication, a replica can lag behind the primary. A user who just edited their profile might briefly see the old version if the read hits a replica.
points: Async: fast writes, possible lag
Sync: no lag, slower writes
Read your own writes from the primary

slides.heading: Failover
slides.subtitle: When the primary dies.
slides.explain: If the primary fails, a replica is promoted to become the new primary. Managed databases can do this automatically.
points: A replica becomes the new primary
Apps reconnect to it
Async setups can lose the latest writes

slides.heading: When to use it
slides.subtitle: Signs you need replicas.
slides.explain: Replication is usually the next step after caching when the database becomes the bottleneck.
points: Read-heavy traffic
High availability needs
Backups without slowing the primary

scenario.situation: A social app's single database handles everything, and feed loads are most of the traffic.
scenario.problem: Read traffic saturates the database, so writes like new posts become slow too.
scenario.fix: Add two read replicas and send feed reads to them. The primary now handles mostly writes, and both get faster.
scenario.takeaway: Replicas scale reads; the primary handles writes.

cta: Have you ever hit a replication lag bug?

title: Database Sharding
intro: Replicas help with reads, but every replica still holds all the data. When the data or the writes outgrow one machine, you shard.

slides.heading: What is sharding?
slides.subtitle: Splitting data across databases.
slides.explain: Sharding splits a big table into pieces called shards, each on its own server. Each shard holds part of the rows, so no single machine stores or writes everything.
points: Each shard holds part of the data
Writes are spread across shards

slides.heading: The shard key
slides.subtitle: How rows are assigned.
slides.explain: The shard key decides which shard a row lives on, for example user_id. A good key spreads data evenly and keeps related data together.
points: Often user_id or tenant_id
Must spread load evenly
Hard to change later

slides.heading: Strategies
slides.subtitle: Ways to split the data.
slides.explain: Range sharding groups nearby keys, which is simple but can create hot spots. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly but makes range queries harder.
points: Range: IDs 1 to 1M on shard 1, and so on
Hash: hash(user_id) decides the shard
Directory: a lookup table maps keys

slides.heading: The downsides
slides.subtitle: Sharding adds real complexity.
slides.explain: Queries across shards, like joins or global counts, become slow and complicated. Moving data when you add shards is also hard.
points: Cross-shard joins are hard
Uneven keys create hot shards
Rebalancing is painful

slides.heading: Before you shard
slides.subtitle: Try cheaper options first.
slides.explain: Indexes, caching, read replicas and bigger machines solve most problems. Sharding is usually the last step.
points: Optimize queries and indexes
Add caching and replicas
Shard when one machine truly can't cope

scenario.situation: A messaging app shards by country, putting each country's users on its own shard.
scenario.problem: One large country has most of the users, so its shard is overloaded while the others sit nearly idle.
scenario.fix: Re-shard by a hash of user_id. Users spread evenly across shards and the hot spot disappears.
scenario.takeaway: Pick a shard key that spreads load evenly.

cta: Have you ever had to shard a database?

title: The CAP Theorem, Simply
intro: In a distributed system, network problems are unavoidable. CAP describes the choice you must make when they happen.

slides.heading: C, A and P
slides.subtitle: Three properties.
slides.explain: Consistency: every read sees the latest write. Availability: every request gets a response. Partition tolerance: the system keeps working when links between nodes fail.
points: C: everyone sees the same data
A: every request gets an answer
P: survives network splits

slides.heading: The real choice
slides.subtitle: During a partition, pick C or A.
slides.explain: Networks do fail, so distributed systems must tolerate partitions. When one happens, a cut-off node must either refuse requests or answer with possibly stale data.
points: Partitions will happen
CP: refuse rather than be wrong
AP: answer, even if stale

slides.heading: CP systems
slides.subtitle: Correctness first.
slides.explain: CP systems return an error or wait rather than show outdated data. Choose this when wrong data is worse than no data.
points: Bank balances
Payments and inventory

slides.heading: AP systems
slides.subtitle: Always respond.
slides.explain: AP systems keep serving and sync up later, which is called eventual consistency. Choose this when staying up matters more than being perfectly current.
points: Social feeds and like counts
Shopping carts

slides.heading: Eventual consistency
slides.subtitle: Correct, just not instantly.
slides.explain: Copies may disagree for a short time, but they converge once updates spread. For likes or view counts, a short delay is fine.
points: Brief disagreement is acceptable
All copies converge over time

scenario.situation: A ticketing site lets two data centers sell seats independently during a network split.
scenario.problem: Both sides keep selling, and the same seat is sold to two different people.
scenario.fix: Treat seat booking as CP: if a data center can't confirm with the other, it pauses sales instead of risking a double booking.
scenario.takeaway: Choose consistency where mistakes are costly.

cta: Would you pick CP or AP for a chat app, and why?

title: Message Queues Explained
intro: Not everything needs to happen while the user waits. Message queues let you do slow work in the background, reliably.

slides.heading: The problem
slides.subtitle: Slow work blocks requests.
slides.explain: If signing up sends an email, resizes an avatar and updates analytics before responding, the user waits for all of it, and one failing step breaks the whole request.
points: Slow responses
One failure breaks everything

slides.heading: What a queue is
slides.subtitle: A to-do list between services.
slides.explain: A producer adds a message to the queue and returns right away. A consumer picks messages up and processes them in the background at its own pace.
points: Producer: adds jobs
Consumer: processes jobs

slides.heading: Benefits
slides.subtitle: Why systems use them.
slides.explain: Queues decouple services so each can scale and fail on its own. They also absorb traffic spikes: messages simply wait until consumers catch up.
points: Faster user-facing responses
Absorbs traffic spikes
Retries when a job fails

slides.heading: Delivery guarantees
slides.subtitle: What happens on failure.
slides.explain: Many queues deliver at least once, so a message can occasionally be processed twice. Consumers should be idempotent: running a job twice has the same effect as once.
points: At-least-once is common
Make consumers idempotent
Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue

slides.heading: Popular tools
slides.subtitle: What teams use.
slides.explain: Pick based on throughput, ordering needs and how much you want to manage yourself.
points: RabbitMQ: classic message broker
Kafka: high-throughput event streams
Amazon SQS: fully managed

scenario.situation: An online store sends the order confirmation email inside the checkout request.
scenario.problem: When the email provider is slow, checkout takes 10 seconds, and when it's down, orders fail completely.
scenario.fix: Checkout saves the order and adds a "send email" message to a queue. A worker sends it in the background and retries if the provider is down.
scenario.takeaway: If the user doesn't need to wait for it, queue it.

cta: Which have you used: RabbitMQ, Kafka or SQS?

title: CDNs: Content Delivery Networks
intro: Your servers might be in one city, but your users are everywhere. A CDN brings content physically closer to them.

slides.heading: The distance problem
slides.subtitle: Data takes time to travel.
slides.explain: A request from Mumbai to a server in the US crosses the world and back. Even over fiber, that distance adds noticeable delay to every file.
points: Far servers mean slow loads
Every image and script pays the cost

slides.heading: What a CDN is
slides.subtitle: Servers around the world.
slides.explain: A CDN is a network of edge servers in many cities. Users are routed to a nearby edge, which serves a cached copy of your content.
points: Edge servers cache your files
The origin is only hit on a cache miss

slides.heading: What to put on it
slides.subtitle: Best for static content.
slides.explain: Files that are the same for everyone are perfect for a CDN. Many CDNs can also cache public API responses and run code at the edge.
points: Images, videos and fonts
CSS and JavaScript bundles
Public, cacheable pages

slides.heading: Cache control
slides.subtitle: Telling the CDN what to keep.
slides.explain: Cache-Control headers decide how long edges keep a file. Hashed filenames like app.3f9a.js let you cache for a year and still ship updates instantly.
points: Long max-age for hashed files
Purge the cache for urgent changes
Don't cache personal data publicly

slides.heading: Extra benefits
slides.subtitle: More than speed.
slides.explain: Because edges absorb most of the traffic, your own servers handle far less. Many CDNs also help absorb DDoS attacks.
points: Less load on your servers
Lower bandwidth costs
DDoS protection

scenario.situation: A startup serves product images from one server in Mumbai, but many customers are in the US and Europe.
scenario.problem: Overseas users wait seconds for each image, and many leave before the page finishes loading.
scenario.fix: Put the images behind a CDN. Overseas users now load them from a nearby edge server instead of from Mumbai.
scenario.takeaway: Serve static files from close to your users.

cta: Which CDN do you use for your projects?

title: Rate Limiting Explained
intro: One buggy client or attacker can flood your API. Rate limiting caps how many requests each client can make.

slides.heading: Why limit?
slides.subtitle: Protect the system for everyone.
slides.explain: Without limits, one script can overload your servers, run up your costs or brute-force passwords. Limits keep the service fair and stable.
points: Stops abuse and brute force
Prevents one client hogging resources
Keeps costs under control

slides.heading: Fixed window
slides.subtitle: Count requests per time window.
slides.explain: Allow N requests per minute and reset the count each minute. It's simple, but a burst at the end of one window plus the start of the next can allow double the limit.
points: Simple to build
Bursts at window edges

slides.heading: Sliding window
slides.subtitle: A smoother count.
slides.explain: Instead of resetting at fixed times, it counts requests over the last rolling minute. This removes the edge-burst problem at the cost of a bit more memory.
points: More accurate limits
Slightly more storage

slides.heading: Token bucket
slides.subtitle: Allows controlled bursts.
slides.explain: Each client has a bucket that refills with tokens at a steady rate. Every request spends a token; when the bucket is empty, requests are rejected until it refills.
points: Allows short bursts
Enforces an average rate
Widely used by public APIs

slides.heading: In practice
slides.subtitle: Where it lives and what it returns.
slides.explain: Rate limiting usually sits at the API gateway or load balancer, with counters in a fast shared store like Redis so every server sees the same count.
points: Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
Add a Retry-After header
Limit per user, API key or IP

scenario.situation: A login endpoint has no limit on attempts.
scenario.problem: An attacker's script tries thousands of passwords per minute against user accounts.
scenario.fix: Limit each IP and account to 5 attempts per minute with a token bucket in Redis, returning 429 when exceeded. Brute force becomes impractical.
scenario.takeaway: Rate limit every public endpoint, especially login.

cta: Have you ever been rate limited by an API?

title: Case Study: Design a URL Shortener
intro: Time to combine everything from this series. Let's design a service like bit.ly, step by step.

slides.heading: Requirements
slides.subtitle: Start with what it must do.
slides.explain: Functional: turn a long URL into a short one, and redirect short links to the original. Non-functional: redirects must be fast and always available.
points: Create short links
Redirect quickly
Reads far outnumber writes

slides.heading: Estimate the scale
slides.subtitle: Rough numbers.
slides.explain: Assume 100 million new links a month, each opened about 100 times. That's roughly 40 writes and 4,000 redirects per second on average.
points: About 40 writes per second
About 4,000 reads per second
Read-heavy: optimize redirects

slides.heading: Short codes
slides.subtitle: Short, unique and compact.
slides.explain: Encode a unique ID in base62, using a-z, A-Z and 0-9. Seven characters give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes, which is plenty.
points: Unique ID from a counter or ID service
Encode it in base62
7 characters is about 3.5 trillion codes

slides.heading: The read path
slides.subtitle: Make redirects fast.
slides.explain: Redirects check a cache first, so popular links rarely touch the database. On a miss, read from a replica and cache the result.
points: Cache hot links in Redis
Read replicas behind the cache
Use 302 if you want to count every click

slides.heading: The full design
slides.subtitle: Putting it together.
slides.explain: A load balancer spreads requests across stateless app servers. Redis caches popular links, a replicated database stores every mapping, and rate limiting protects link creation.
points: Stateless servers scale out
Cache and replicas handle reads
Rate limit creation to stop spam

scenario.situation: The shortener launches and one link goes viral, getting millions of clicks in an hour.
scenario.problem: If every click queried the database, that single hot row could overwhelm it.
scenario.fix: After the first click, the link is served from the Redis cache, so the database barely notices the spike.
scenario.takeaway: Design for your heaviest path: here, the redirect.

cta: What should we design next in this series?

title: Types of APIs Explained Simply
intro: APIs are the backbone of modern applications. They help different software systems communicate and share data seamlessly.

slides.heading: REST API
slides.subtitle: The most widely used API type.
points: Uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
Lightweight and easy to use
Returns data mostly in JSON format

slides.heading: SOAP API
slides.subtitle: A protocol for secure, structured communication.
points: Uses XML format for messages
Highly secure with built-in error handling
Common in enterprise applications

slides.heading: GraphQL API
slides.subtitle: Ask for exactly the data you need.
points: Single endpoint for all queries
Client decides the response shape
Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching

slides.heading: WebSocket API
slides.subtitle: Two-way communication that stays open.
points: Persistent connection between client and server
Server can push data without a new request
Much lower latency than polling

slides.heading: gRPC API
slides.subtitle: Fast, typed communication between services.
points: Uses Protocol Buffers, not JSON
Much faster than REST for service-to-service calls
Strict, strongly-typed contracts

cta: Which API have you used the most? Let me know in the comments.

title: HTTP Status Codes You Must Know
intro: Every API response carries a status code. Knowing what they mean saves hours of debugging.

slides.heading: 2xx Success
slides.subtitle: The request worked as expected.
points: 200 OK — standard successful response
201 Created — a new resource was made
204 No Content — success, nothing to return

slides.heading: 3xx Redirection
slides.subtitle: The resource moved somewhere else.
points: 301 Moved Permanently — update your bookmarks
302 Found — temporary redirect
304 Not Modified — use your cached copy

slides.heading: 4xx Client Error
slides.subtitle: The request itself was the problem.
points: 400 Bad Request — malformed input
401 Unauthorized — you're not logged in
403 Forbidden — logged in, but not allowed
404 Not Found — the resource doesn't exist

slides.heading: 5xx Server Error
slides.subtitle: The request was fine, the server wasn't.
points: 500 Internal Server Error — something crashed
502 Bad Gateway — upstream server failed
503 Service Unavailable — server is overloaded

cta: Which status code do you see the most in your logs?

title: SQL JOINs Explained Simply
intro: JOINs combine rows from two or more tables. Pick the wrong one and you either lose data or duplicate it.

slides.heading: INNER JOIN
slides.subtitle: Only rows that match in both tables.
points: Returns rows where the join condition is true in both tables
Rows with no match on either side are excluded
The most commonly used join
examples: Orders that have a matching customer

slides.heading: LEFT JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from the left table, matched or not.
points: Keeps all rows from the left table
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL
Useful for finding what's missing
examples: All customers, even those with zero orders

slides.heading: RIGHT JOIN
slides.subtitle: The mirror image of LEFT JOIN.
points: Keeps all rows from the right table
Unmatched left-side columns come back as NULL
Rarely used — most people rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN
examples: All products, even unordered ones, from the orders table

slides.heading: FULL JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from both tables.
points: Combines LEFT and RIGHT JOIN results
Unmatched rows from either side get NULLs
Good for finding mismatches between two tables
examples: Reconciling two systems that should be in sync

cta: Which JOIN trips you up the most?

title: Git Commands Every Developer Needs
intro: You don't need 100 git commands memorized. These cover 90% of daily work.

slides.heading: Starting out
slides.subtitle: Get a project under version control.
points: git init — start tracking a new project
git clone <url> — copy an existing repo
git status — see what's changed

slides.heading: Saving work
slides.subtitle: Record changes as commits.
points: git add <file> — stage a change
git commit -m "message" — save staged changes
git push — send commits to the remote

slides.heading: Branching
slides.subtitle: Work on features without breaking main.

title: How Caching Actually Works

slides.heading: Database Cache

scenario.problem: Bots scan public repos for keys. Someone finds it and runs up charges on the account.
scenario.fix: Revoke the key, put the new one in an environment variable, add .env to .gitignore and read it with process.env.
scenario.takeaway: Secrets go in environment variables, never in code.

cta: Have you ever accidentally committed a secret?

title: CORS Errors Explained Simply
intro: Seen "blocked by CORS policy" in your console? Here's what's actually happening and how to fix it.

slides.heading: Same-origin policy
slides.subtitle: The browser's default rule.
points: Origin = protocol + domain + port
Pages can't read responses from other origins by default
It protects users from malicious sites

slides.heading: What CORS is
slides.subtitle: A way for servers to opt in.
points: The server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin
The browser checks it before sharing the response
The server decides, not the frontend

slides.heading: Preflight requests
slides.subtitle: The browser asks first.
points: An OPTIONS request sent before some requests
Triggered by methods like PUT or custom headers
The server must reply with what it allows

slides.heading: How to fix it
slides.subtitle: Fix it on the server.
points: Configure CORS in your backend
Allow specific origins, especially with cookies
Use a dev-server proxy during local development

scenario.situation: Your React app on localhost:5173 calls your API on localhost:3000.
scenario.problem: The browser blocks the response with a CORS error, even though the same request works in Postman.
scenario.fix: Allow that origin on the API, for example in Express: app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173" })).
scenario.takeaway: CORS is fixed on the server, not the frontend.

cta: How many hours has CORS cost you?

title: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage
intro: Three ways to store data in the browser, each built for a different job.

slides.heading: Cookies
slides.subtitle: Small data sent with requests.
points: About 4KB per cookie
Sent to the server automatically
Can be httpOnly so JavaScript can't read them

slides.heading: localStorage
slides.subtitle: Browser storage that persists.
points: Around 5MB per site in most browsers
Stays until it's cleared
Readable by any script on the page

slides.heading: sessionStorage
slides.subtitle: Storage for a single tab.
points: Same API as localStorage
Cleared when the tab closes
Not shared between tabs

slides.heading: Security tip
slides.subtitle: Choose storage carefully.
points: Never store passwords in the browser
Prefer httpOnly cookies for auth tokens
Treat stored data as user-editable

scenario.situation: An app stores the user's login token in localStorage.
scenario.problem: An XSS bug lets an injected script read localStorage and send the token to an attacker.
scenario.fix: Keep the session in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. JavaScript can't read it, so XSS can't steal it.
scenario.takeaway: Keep auth tokens out of JavaScript's reach.

cta: Where do you store auth tokens in your apps?

title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases Explained
intro: Both store data, but in very different ways. The right choice depends on your data and how you read it.

slides.heading: SQL databases
slides.subtitle: Tables with a fixed schema.
points: Rows and columns, like a spreadsheet
Relationships through joins
Strong consistency with transactions

slides.heading: NoSQL databases
slides.subtitle: Flexible data models.
points: Document, key-value, graph or wide-column
Schema can change easily
Often built to scale across many servers

slides.heading: Pick SQL when
slides.subtitle: Structure and correctness matter.
points: Your data is highly related
Correctness is critical, like payments
You need complex queries and reports

slides.heading: Pick NoSQL when
slides.subtitle: Flexibility and scale matter.
points: The data shape changes often
You mostly read data by a single key
You need very high write volume

scenario.situation: A team builds a banking app on a document database because it felt quicker to start.
scenario.problem: A transfer updates two accounts, and keeping both balances consistent becomes complicated and error-prone.
scenario.fix: Use a relational database with transactions. Both updates succeed together or fail together.
scenario.takeaway: Choose by your data and its rules, not by hype.

cta: SQL or NoSQL for your current project?

title: Database Indexes Explained Simply
intro: An index works like the index in a book: it lets the database find rows without reading every page.

slides.heading: Without an index
slides.subtitle: The database reads every row.
points: Called a full table scan
Gets slow as tables grow

slides.heading: With an index
slides.subtitle: Jump straight to the right rows.
points: Usually stored as a sorted B-tree
Lookups take a few steps, not millions
Speeds up WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY

slides.heading: The trade-off
slides.subtitle: Indexes aren't free.
points: Each index uses extra storage
Inserts and updates get slower
Index the columns you actually query

slides.heading: Check your query
slides.subtitle: Don't guess, measure.
points: Run EXPLAIN to see the query plan
A full scan on a big table hints at a missing index
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);

scenario.situation: Your login query, SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?, gets slower as the app reaches a million users.
scenario.problem: There's no index on email, so the database scans every row on every single login.
scenario.fix: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email); lets the database jump straight to the matching row.
scenario.takeaway: Index the columns you search by.

cta: Have you ever fixed a slow query with one index?

title: Core Web Vitals Explained Simply
intro: Google's three metrics for how fast and smooth your page feels to real users.

slides.heading: LCP
slides.subtitle: Largest Contentful Paint: loading.
points: Time until the main content appears
Good: 2.5 seconds or less
Fix: optimize images, use a CDN

slides.heading: INP
slides.subtitle: Interaction to Next Paint: responsiveness.
points: How fast the page responds to clicks and taps
Good: 200 milliseconds or less
Fix: break up long JavaScript tasks

slides.heading: CLS
slides.subtitle: Cumulative Layout Shift: stability.
points: How much the layout jumps while loading
Good: 0.1 or less
Fix: set image sizes, reserve space for ads

slides.heading: Measure it
slides.subtitle: Free tools to check your site.
points: Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools
PageSpeed Insights for real-user data
The web-vitals library for your own analytics

scenario.situation: A blog's mobile LCP is 4.8 seconds, well above the 2.5 second target.
scenario.problem: The hero image is a 3 MB PNG, so the main content takes a long time to appear.
scenario.fix: Convert it to WebP, size it for the screen and preload it. That alone can bring LCP under 2.5 seconds.
scenario.takeaway: Oversized images are a top cause of slow LCP.

cta: What's your site's LCP right now?

title: Web Accessibility Basics Every Dev Should Know
intro: Accessible sites work for everyone, including people using screen readers, keyboards or zoom.

slides.heading: Alt text
slides.subtitle: Describe your images.
points: Screen readers read alt text aloud
Describe the purpose, not just the look
Use alt="" for purely decorative images

slides.heading: Keyboard access
slides.subtitle: Not everyone uses a mouse.
points: Everything clickable works with Tab and Enter
Keep a visible focus outline
Use real <button> and <a> elements

slides.heading: Color contrast
slides.subtitle: Make text easy to read.
points: WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text
Don't rely on color alone to show meaning
Test with a contrast checker

slides.heading: Forms
slides.subtitle: Where accessibility breaks most often.
points: Every input needs a <label>
Error messages should say how to fix it
Placeholder text is not a label

scenario.situation: A checkout form uses grey placeholder text instead of labels.
scenario.problem: Screen reader users can't tell what each field is, and the hint disappears as soon as anyone types.
scenario.fix: Add a visible <label for="email"> to every input, and keep placeholders for examples only.
scenario.takeaway: Every input needs a real label.

cta: Have you ever tried using your site with only a keyboard?

title: Why Developers Love TypeScript
intro: TypeScript is JavaScript with types. It catches many bugs before your code ever runs.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.subtitle: JavaScript plus a type system.
points: Compiles to plain JavaScript
Types are checked, then removed at build time
You can adopt it gradually

slides.heading: Basic types
slides.subtitle: The building blocks.
points: string, number and boolean
string[] for an array of strings
Unions: "admin" | "user"

slides.heading: Interfaces
slides.subtitle: Describe the shape of objects.
points: interface User { id: number; name: string }
Your editor autocompletes properties
Typos in property names become errors

slides.heading: Why it helps
slides.subtitle: Benefits you feel every day.
points: Catches bugs while you type
Makes refactoring much safer
Works as living documentation

scenario.situation: Your backend renames user.fullName to user.name.
scenario.problem: In plain JavaScript, every screen still reading fullName quietly shows undefined in production.
scenario.fix: With a User interface, update the type once and the compiler points to every line still using fullName.
scenario.takeaway: Types turn runtime surprises into compile errors.

cta: Do you write TypeScript or plain JavaScript?

title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E Testing
intro: Different tests catch different bugs. The testing pyramid shows how to balance them.

slides.heading: Unit tests
slides.subtitle: Test one small piece in isolation.
points: Fast and cheap to run
Test a single function or component
Should be most of your tests

slides.heading: Integration tests
slides.subtitle: Test pieces working together.
points: Check modules work correctly together
Often include a real database or API
Slower than unit tests
examples: An API endpoint with its database

slides.heading: E2E tests
slides.subtitle: Test the app like a real user.
points: Run in a real browser
Catch issues across the whole stack
Slowest and most fragile, so keep them few

slides.heading: The pyramid
slides.subtitle: How to balance them.
points: Many unit tests at the base
Fewer integration tests in the middle
A handful of E2E tests on top

scenario.situation: A refactor of the discount function accidentally breaks coupons above 50%.
scenario.problem: Nobody notices until customers start reporting wrong prices.
scenario.fix: A few unit tests for calculateDiscount() would have failed instantly, before the change was merged.
scenario.takeaway: Unit test your business logic first.

cta: Which kind of test do you write the most?

title: Responsive Design Basics
intro: Most visitors browse on phones. These basics make your site look good on every screen size.

slides.heading: Viewport meta tag
slides.subtitle: Step one for mobile.
points: Tells phones to use the device's real width
Without it, pages render zoomed out
Goes in the <head> of every page

slides.heading: Mobile first
slides.subtitle: Start small, then scale up.
points: Write base styles for small screens
Add min-width media queries for bigger ones
Usually leads to simpler CSS

slides.heading: Media queries
slides.subtitle: Change the layout at breakpoints.
points: @media (min-width: 768px) { ... }
Switch columns, sizes or visibility
Add breakpoints where your design breaks

slides.heading: Flexible media
slides.subtitle: Images that never overflow.
points: img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
Use srcset to serve different image sizes
Prefer fluid widths over fixed pixels

scenario.situation: Your site looks perfect on desktop, but on a phone the text is tiny and users have to zoom.
scenario.problem: The viewport meta tag is missing, so the phone renders the page at desktop width and shrinks it.
scenario.fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> and build the layout mobile first.
scenario.takeaway: The viewport tag is step one for mobile.

cta: Do you design mobile first or desktop first?

title: How to Debug Like a Pro
intro: Debugging is a skill you can learn. This process works for almost any bug.

slides.heading: Read the error
slides.subtitle: It often tells you exactly what's wrong.
points: Read the whole message, not just the first line
The stack trace shows where it happened
Find the first line from your own code

slides.heading: Reproduce it
slides.subtitle: Make it happen on demand.
points: Find the exact steps that trigger it
Shrink it to the smallest failing case
A bug you can reproduce is half fixed

slides.heading: Use your tools
slides.subtitle: Stop guessing, start looking.
points: Set breakpoints in DevTools or your editor
Log values at key points
Check the Network tab for failed requests

slides.heading: Search smart
slides.subtitle: Someone has probably seen it before.
points: Search the exact error message
Check the official docs and GitHub issues
Explain the problem out loud, step by step

scenario.situation: Your app crashes with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')".
scenario.problem: You start changing random code, hoping the error goes away.
scenario.fix: The stack trace points to your line. Logging the value shows the API returned nothing. Fix: (data ?? []).map(...).
scenario.takeaway: Read the error, find the line, check the value.

cta: What's the longest you've spent on a single bug?

title: The 4 Pillars of Object-Oriented Programming
intro: OOP shows up in interviews and in languages like Java, Python and C#. Here are the four core ideas in plain words.

slides.heading: Encapsulation
slides.subtitle: Keep data and behavior together.
points: Bundle data with the methods that use it
Hide internal details behind a clear interface

slides.heading: Abstraction
slides.subtitle: Show only what matters.
points: Expose simple methods, hide the complexity
Like driving a car without knowing the engine

slides.heading: Inheritance
slides.subtitle: Reuse code from a parent class.
points: A child class extends a parent class
Shares behavior without copying it
Use it only for true "is-a" relationships

slides.heading: Polymorphism
slides.subtitle: One interface, many forms.
points: Different classes answer the same method
Code works with any object that fits

scenario.situation: A payment app supports cards and now needs UPI and PayPal too.
scenario.problem: One giant function with an if/else for every payment type gets harder to change with each new method.
scenario.fix: Create a Payment interface with pay(). Card, UPI and PayPal each implement it, and checkout just calls pay().
scenario.takeaway: Polymorphism lets you add new types without editing old code.

cta: Which pillar was hardest to understand at first?
